Rewrite the following essay substantively. Aim for 1355 words; the acceptable range is 1084-1500 words, and the corpus-wide hard range is 800-1500 words. Use at least 6 natural paragraphs, preferably approximately 19 paragraphs. Do not include a heading.

SOURCE ESSAY:
We have all met the man who says that some odd things have happened to him, but that he does not really believe that they were supernatural. My own position is the opposite of this. I believe in the supernatural as a matter of intellect and reason, not as a matter of personal experience. I do not see ghosts; I only see their inherent probability. But it is entirely a matter of the mere intelligence, not even of the motions; my nerves and body are altogether of this earth, very earthy. But upon people of this temperament one weird incident will often leave a peculiar impression. And the weirdest circumstance that ever occurred to me occurred a little while ago. It consisted in nothing less than my playing a game, and playing it quite well for some seventeen consecutive minutes. The ghost of my grandfather would have astonished me less.

On one of these blue and burning afternoons I found myself, to my inexpressible astonishment, playing a game called croquet. I had imagined that it belonged to the epoch of Leach and Anthony Trollope, and I had neglected to provide myself with those very long and luxuriant side whiskers which are really essential to such a scene. I played it with a man whom we will call Parkinson, and with whom I had a semi-philosophical argument which lasted through the entire contest. It is deeply implanted in my mind that I had the best of the argument; but it is certain and beyond dispute that I had the worst of the game.

“Oh, Parkinson, Parkinson!” I cried, patting him affectionately on the head with a mallet, “how far you really are from the pure love of the sport—you who can play. It is only we who play badly who love the Game itself. You love glory; you love applause; you love the earthquake voice of victory; you do not love croquet. You do not love croquet until you love being beaten at croquet. It is we the bunglers who adore the occupation in the abstract. It is we to whom it is art for art’s sake. If we may see the face of Croquet herself (if I may so express myself) we are content to see her face turned upon us in anger. Our play is called amateurish; and we wear proudly the name of amateur, for amateurs is but the French for Lovers. We accept all adventures from our Lady, the most disastrous or the most dreary. We wait outside her iron gates (I allude to the hoops), vainly essaying to enter. Our devoted balls, impetuous and full of chivalry, will not be confined within the pedantic boundaries of the mere croquet ground. Our balls seek honour in the ends of the earth; they turn up in the flower-beds and the conservatory; they are to be found in the front garden and the next street. No, Parkinson! The good painter has skill. It is the bad painter who loves his art. The good musician loves being a musician, the bad musician loves music. With such a pure and hopeless passion do I worship croquet. I love the game itself. I love the parallelogram of grass marked out with chalk or tape, as if its limits were the frontiers of my sacred Fatherland, the four seas of Britain. I love the mere swing of the mallets, and the click of the balls is music. The four colours are to me sacramental and symbolic, like the red of martyrdom, or the white of Easter Day. You lose all this, my poor Parkinson. You have to solace yourself for the absence of this vision by the paltry consolation of being able to go through hoops and to hit the stick.”

And I waved my mallet in the air with a graceful gaiety.

“Don’t be too sorry for me,” said Parkinson, with his simple sarcasm. “I shall get over it in time. But it seems to me that the more a man likes a game the better he would want to play it. Granted that the pleasure in the thing itself comes first, does not the pleasure of success come naturally and inevitably afterwards? Or, take your own simile of the Knight and his Lady-love. I admit the gentleman does first and foremost want to be in the lady’s presence. But I never yet heard of a gentleman who wanted to look an utter ass when he was there.”

“Perhaps not; though he generally looks it,” I replied. “But the truth is that there is a fallacy in the simile, although it was my own. The happiness at which the lover is aiming is an infinite happiness, which can be extended without limit. The more he is loved, normally speaking, the jollier he will be. It is definitely true that the stronger the love of both lovers, the stronger will be the happiness. But it is not true that the stronger the play of both croquet players the stronger will be the game. It is logically possible—(follow me closely here, Parkinson!)—it is logically possible, to play croquet too well to enjoy it at all. If you could put this blue ball through that distant hoop as easily as you could pick it up with your hand, then you would not put it through that hoop any more than you pick it up with your hand; it would not be worth doing. If you could play unerringly you would not play at all. The moment the game is perfect the game disappears.”

“I do not think, however,” said Parkinson, “that you are in any immediate danger of effecting that sort of destruction. I do not think your croquet will vanish through its own faultless excellence. You are safe for the present.”

I again caressed him with the mallet, knocked a ball about, wired myself, and resumed the thread of my discourse.

The long, warm evening had been gradually closing in, and by this time it was almost twilight. By the time I had delivered four more fundamental principles, and my companion had gone through five more hoops, the dusk was verging upon dark.

“We shall have to give this up,” said Parkinson, as he missed a ball almost for the first time, “I can’t see a thing.”

“Nor can I,” I answered, “and it is a comfort to reflect that I could not hit anything if I saw it.”

With that I struck a ball smartly, and sent it away into the darkness towards where the shadowy figure of Parkinson moved in the hot haze. Parkinson immediately uttered a loud and dramatic cry. The situation, indeed, called for it. I had hit the right ball.

Stunned with astonishment, I crossed the gloomy ground, and hit my ball again. It went through a hoop. I could not see the hoop; but it was the right hoop. I shuddered from head to foot.

Words were wholly inadequate, so I slouched heavily after that impossible ball. Again I hit it away into the night, in what I supposed was the vague direction of the quite invisible stick. And in the dead silence I heard the stick rattle as the ball struck it heavily.

I threw down my mallet. “I can’t stand this,” I said. “My ball has gone right three times. These things are not of this world.”

“Pick your mallet up,” said Parkinson, “have another go.”

“I tell you I daren’t. If I made another hoop like that I should see all the devils dancing there on the blessed grass.”

“Why devils?” asked Parkinson; “they may be only fairies making fun of you. They are sending you the ‘Perfect Game,’ which is no game.”

I looked about me. The garden was full of a burning darkness, in which the faint glimmers had the look of fire. I stepped across the grass as if it burnt me, picked up the mallet, and hit the ball somewhere—somewhere where another ball might be. I heard the dull click of the balls touching, and ran into the house like one pursued.

message.content:
We’ve all encountered individuals who recount strange occurrences with a skeptical tone, insisting that despite the oddities, they do not believe in the supernatural. In stark contrast, I find myself firmly grounded in the belief of the supernatural, rooted in intellect and reason rather than personal encounters. I don’t perceive ghosts; instead, I recognize their intrinsic likelihood. My understanding is purely cerebral; my physical being is firmly tethered to this world. Yet, it is often the most peculiar experiences that leave a lasting impression on those of my mindset. The most bizarre event I have ever encountered unfolded recently, centering around my ability to engage in a game—one that I played surprisingly well for a solid seventeen minutes. I daresay, even the ghost of my grandfather would have evoked less astonishment.

On one of those brilliant, scorching afternoons, I found myself, to my utter disbelief, participating in a game of croquet. I had always assumed this pastime was a relic of the days of Leach and Anthony Trollope, and thus I had neglected to don the extravagant side whiskers that seem essential for such an occasion. I played alongside a man I shall refer to as Parkinson; our match was accompanied by a semi-philosophical debate that persisted throughout the duration of the game. I am convinced that I held the upper hand in our discussions, yet it is undeniable that I was thoroughly outmatched in the game itself.

“Oh, Parkinson, Parkinson!” I exclaimed, affectionately tapping him on the head with my mallet. “You are so far removed from the pure love of the sport! You, who can actually play! It is we, the inept, who find joy in the essence of the game. You crave glory; you seek the thunderous applause of victory; you do not truly love croquet. You cannot profess your love for the game until you have embraced the possibility of defeat in croquet. It is we, the bunglers, who worship the sport for its own sake. If we could glimpse the face of Croquet herself—if I may put it that way—we would be content to see her expression of displeasure. Our play is labeled as amateurish, yet we wear that title with pride, for 'amateur' derives from the French word for 'lover.' We accept all the encounters she offers, whether they lead to disaster or monotony. We linger outside her iron gates—those hoops, if you will—striving to gain entry. Our devoted balls, eager and chivalrous, refuse to be confined within the rigid confines of the croquet lawn. They seek honor in the far reaches of the earth; they end up in flower beds, conservatories, front gardens, and even in neighboring streets. No, Parkinson! A skilled painter possesses technique; it is the unskilled painter who cherishes his art. A proficient musician revels in his craft, while the mediocre musician loves music itself. With a pure and unrelenting passion, I revere croquet. I adore the game for its own sake. I cherish the rectangular patch of grass outlined by chalk or tape, as if its boundaries represent the frontiers of my sacred homeland, the four seas of Britain. I delight in the simple swing of the mallet, while the sound of the balls colliding is like music to my ears. The four colors resonate deeply with me, each symbolizing something profound, akin to the red of martyrdom or the white of Easter Sunday. You miss all of this, dear Parkinson. To comfort yourself for the absence of this vision, you resort to the trivial consolation of successfully navigating hoops and striking the stick.”

With that, I flourished my mallet with a lighthearted elegance.

“Don’t lament my fate too much,” Parkinson replied, his tone tinged with playful sarcasm. “I’ll recover from this in due time. However, it strikes me that the more one enjoys a game, the more one wishes to excel at it. While the pleasure derived from the activity itself is paramount, doesn’t the satisfaction of success naturally follow? Consider your own analogy of the Knight and his Lady-love. Admittedly, the gentleman’s foremost desire is to be in the presence of the lady. Yet, I’ve never heard of a gentleman who would want to appear foolish in her company.”

“Perhaps not; though he often ends up looking foolish,” I countered. “However, therein lies a flaw in the analogy, despite it being my own creation. The joy sought by the lover is a boundless happiness that can expand infinitely. Generally speaking, the more he is loved, the happier he becomes. It’s true that the deeper the love shared between both lovers, the greater the joy will be. Yet, it’s not the case that the better both croquet players perform, the more enjoyable the game becomes. It is entirely feasible—(stay with me here, Parkinson!)—to play croquet too well to actually derive pleasure from it. If you could send that blue ball through that distant hoop as easily as picking it up with your hand, you would not bother to do it; it would lose its significance. If you could play flawlessly, you would cease to play altogether. Once the game reaches perfection, it ceases to exist.”

“I don’t believe, however,” Parkinson interjected, “that you are in any immediate danger of achieving that level of perfection. I doubt your croquet will vanish due to its own excellence. You’re safe for now.”

Once again, I affectionately tapped him with the mallet, sent a ball flying, and picked up where I left off in our discussion.

As the long, warm evening gradually descended, twilight was settling in. By the time I articulated four more fundamental principles, and Parkinson managed to navigate five additional hoops, the encroaching darkness was almost complete.

“We’ll have to call it a night,” Parkinson said, missing a ball for what seemed like the first time. “I can’t see a thing.”

“Neither can I,” I replied, “and it’s somewhat comforting to recognize that I couldn’t hit anything even if I could see it.”

With that, I struck the ball decisively, sending it off into the darkness toward the hazy shape of Parkinson. He let out a loud and dramatic exclamation. The situation indeed warranted such a response, as I had struck the correct ball.

Astonished, I traversed the dimly lit ground and hit my ball again. It rolled through a hoop. I couldn’t see the hoop, but I was certain it was the right one. A shiver ran through my body.

Words escaped me, so I trudged heavily after that incredible ball. Once more, I struck it into the night, believing I was aiming in the general direction of another ball. In the oppressive silence, I heard the dull thud as the ball made contact with the stick.

I dropped my mallet, exclaiming, “I can’t endure this! My ball has gone through the hoop three times. These phenomena are not of this realm.”

“Pick up your mallet,” Parkinson urged, “and give it another try.”

“I refuse to. If I were to accomplish another hoop like that, I’d be confronted by a legion of devils dancing on the blessed grass.”

“Why devils?” Parkinson questioned. “They could be merely fairies having their fun. They’re bestowing upon you the ‘Perfect Game,’ which is no game at all.”

I glanced around, the garden enveloped in an intense darkness, where the faint glimmers appeared almost like flames. I stepped gingerly across the grass, as though it were on fire, retrieved the mallet, and struck the ball somewhere—anywhere another ball might be. I heard the dull clack of the balls colliding and dashed into the house as if I were being pursued.
